summary: Lists IANA considerations for RPC network identifiers and universal addresses. It updates, but does not replace, RFC 1833.

eli5.summary: This explains the official list of names for networks and addresses that remote-procedure programs use.

subtitle: IANA registries for RPC network identifiers and universal address formats.

tldr.problem: RPC systems need a way to identify different networks and represent addresses in a universal format, but RFC 1833 did not specify how these identifiers and formats should be registered centrally.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC creates IANA registries for RPC network identifiers (netids) and RPC universal address (uaddr) formats, and populates them with netids for common transports like TCP, UDP, SCTP, and RDMA.
tldr.outcome: Systems that rely on consistent netids and address formats—such as NFSv4 and RPC/RDMA—can now use standardized identifiers across implementations.

facts.value: 8 (tcp, tcp6, udp, udp6, sctp, sctp6, rdma, rdma6)

today: RFC 5665 updated RFC 1833 to establish formal registries for RPC network identifiers and address formats. These registries continue to be used by protocols like NFSv4 and RPC/RDMA to ensure consistent netid and address representation across implementations.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Remote Procedure Call (RPC) is a protocol that lets one program call functions on a remote machine. RFC 1833 introduced the concept of a network identifier (netid) and a universal address (uaddr) as a way to distinguish between different transport protocols and represent addresses in a canonical form.

However, RFC 1833 left netids to be defined by system administrators based on local conventions, which caused inconsistency across systems. More recent protocols like Network File System version 4 (NFSv4) and RPC/RDMA depend on consistent netid and uaddr values across multiple implementations. This RFC standardizes netids and uaddr formats by creating two IANA registries and specifying their initial contents.
sections.eli5: RPC lets programs talk to other programs over a network. Each network type needs a name (a netid) and a standard way to write addresses on that network (a uaddr). This RFC made an official list of those names and formats.

sections.title: Network Identifiers and Universal Addresses
sections.content:
A network identifier (netid) is a short string that names a transport protocol and network combination, such as tcp, udp, or tcp6 (TCP over IPv6). The netid lets RPC code specify which network to use when calling a remote function.

A universal address (uaddr) is a text representation of a network address that works across different systems. For IPv4 TCP, the uaddr format is the IP address in dotted-decimal notation followed by the port number, each part separated by a period: 192.0.2.7.203.81 represents IP address 192.0.2.7 and port 52049.
sections.eli5: A netid is a name for a type of network connection, like "tcp" or "udp". A uaddr is a way to write an address on that network so any computer can read it the same way.

sections.title: The Netid Registry
sections.content:
The IANA Netid Registry contains entries for all registered network identifiers. Each entry includes the netid name, a constant name (prefixed with NC_) for use in programming, a description, a point of contact, and a cross-reference to the corresponding uaddr format in the format registry.

Netids assigned through Standards Action are 1 to 8 characters and include common protocols: tcp, tcp6, udp, udp6, sctp, sctp6, rdma, and rdma6. First Come First Served netids are 9 to 128 characters. Reserved prefixes like "STDS", "FCFS", "PRIV", "EXPE", and "ICMP" are not available for assignment, and netids containing a dot are reserved for possible future hierarchical allocation.
sections.eli5: The netid registry is an official list of names for different network types. Standard ones like TCP and UDP are short, and new ones can be longer if they're registered on a first-come, first-served basis.

sections.title: Universal Address Formats
sections.content:
The IANA Uaddr Format Registry specifies how addresses are represented for each netid. Different transport protocols may have different address formats depending on whether they operate over IPv4 or IPv6.

For IPv4 transports that use 16-bit port numbers (TCP, UDP, SCTP, RDMA), the uaddr format is six decimal numbers separated by periods: h1.h2.h3.h4.p1.p2, where h1 through h4 are the octets of the IPv4 address and p1, p2 encode the 16-bit port number in big-endian order.

For IPv6 transports with 16-bit port numbers, the format uses the standard IPv6 address notation followed by port octets: x1:x2:x3:x4:x5:x6:x7:x8.p1.p2. System V loopback transports use an opaque octet string, and some special netids like "-" have no address format.
sections.eli5: A uaddr is a text string that represents where a computer and port are. For IPv4, it's the IP address and port separated by periods. For IPv6, it's the IPv6 address and port.

sections.title: SCTP Network Handling
sections.content:
The Stream Control Transmission Protocol (SCTP) has a special interaction with RPC. When using the sctp or sctp6 netids, the ONC RPC Record Marking standard (defined in RFC 5531) is not used. Instead, SCTP's native record-oriented data transfer mechanism is used directly.

Additionally, port 2049 is assigned to NFS over SCTP for both the sctp and sctp6 netids, allowing NFS to operate efficiently over SCTP in both IPv4 and IPv6 environments.
sections.eli5: SCTP is a network protocol that can be used with RPC, but it doesn't use RPC's usual record marking system. Instead, it uses its own message format. Port 2049 is reserved for NFS running over SCTP.

sections.title: Registration Policies
sections.content:
The netid and format registries have two different paths for new registrations: Standards Action and First Come First Served (FCFS). Standards Action assignments are made through the IETF standards process for important, widely-used protocols. The IESG must approve these assignments, and they use short netid names.

FCFS assignments can be made by anyone meeting the minimal requirements and can use longer netid names. Each FCFS assignment must include a point of contact with an email address, a description of the netid and its use, and a reference to any underlying protocol specifications.

Registrants can update their own FCFS registrations, and the IESG can update any registration when the point of contact is unavailable or when RFC 1833 is updated in ways that affect the registration requirements.
sections.eli5: Standards Action is for important protocols that go through the IETF approval process. First Come First Served is for anyone who can show their netid is being used. Both types can be updated later if things change.

sections.title: Initial Registry Content
sections.content:
The registries are initialized with ten netids and four uaddr formats. The netids include the loopback transports (ticlts, ticots, ticotsord) which are legacy System V mechanisms, the no-protocol netid (a single hyphen) and eight Standards Action netids for modern transports: tcp, tcp6, udp, udp6, sctp, sctp6, rdma, and rdma6.

The uaddr format registry contains four entries: the System V loopback format, the format for the no-protocol netid, the IPv4 16-bit port format used by TCP/UDP/SCTP/RDMA, and the IPv6 16-bit port format for the same transports.
sections.eli5: The registries start with a dozen network types that are commonly used, like TCP and UDP, and the standard ways to write addresses on each type of network.

sections.title: Status Today
sections.content: RFC 5665 updates RFC 1833 but does not replace it. The netid and uaddr registries it creates are maintained by IANA and continue to accept new registrations according to the Standards Action and First Come First Served policies. NFSv4 and RPC/RDMA rely on the consistency these registries provide.
sections.eli5: The registries RFC 5665 created are still used today. Whenever someone wants to use RPC with a new network type, they register a new netid and uaddr format here.

data.title: IPv4 TCP address
data.code:
192.0.2.7.203.81

Breaks down to:
192.0.2.7     = IPv4 address
203           = high byte of port
81            = low byte of port
              = port 52049 (203 times 256 plus 81)
